title: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport: Broker Liability in 2026
summary: The Supreme Court ruled 9-0 that brokers can be sued for negligent carrier selection. What Montgomery decided, where it stands, and what to check.
body_markdown:
In Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, the Supreme Court ruled on May 14, 2026 that federal law does not block state negligent-selection claims against freight brokers \[1\]. If a carrier you hire causes a crash, the injured party can now argue in court that you should not have hired that carrier.


The vote was 9-0. The decision did not say what a broker must do to choose a carrier with reasonable care. State courts and juries will decide that, case by case, and they will look at what the broker checked.


This article is general information for freight brokers. It is not legal advice. Talk to your own counsel about your contracts and your exposure.


## What happened in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport


Shawn Montgomery had stopped his tractor-trailer on the shoulder of an Illinois highway. A truck driving for the motor carrier Caribe Transport II veered off the road and hit him. Montgomery lost his leg \[1\].


C.H. Robinson had brokered the load to Caribe Transport. Montgomery sued the driver, the carrier, and the broker. His claim against the broker was negligent hiring: he said that Caribe Transport had a "conditional" safety rating from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) when the broker hired it, with deficiencies in driver qualification, hours of service, maintenance, and crash rate. So the broker knew, or should have known, that the carrier was likely to cause a crash \[1\].


The district court and the Seventh Circuit dismissed the claim against the broker. They said a federal law, the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act (FAAAA), preempted it \[1\].


## What the Supreme Court decided


The FAAAA stops states from enforcing laws "related to a price, route, or service" of a motor carrier or broker. But it has a safety exception: it does not restrict "the safety regulatory authority of a State with respect to motor vehicles" \[1\]\[2\].


The question was whether a negligent-selection claim against a broker falls inside that safety exception. Justice Barrett, for a unanimous Court, said it does. Requiring a broker to use ordinary care when it selects a carrier "concerns" motor vehicles, "most obviously, the trucks that will transport the goods" \[1\]. The Court reversed the Seventh Circuit and sent the case back for further proceedings \[1\]\[3\].


Three limits are worth knowing:


- State laws about carrier prices, routes, and services that have no relation to safety are still preempted \[1\].
- The Court did not decide what reasonable care in carrier selection means. That comes from each state's negligence law.
- The plaintiff still has to prove negligence and causation. The ruling only lets the claim proceed.


### What the concurrence tells brokers


Justice Kavanaugh, joined by Justice Alito, wrote separately. He said the decision "should not be read to mean that brokers will routinely be subject to state tort liability in the wake of truck accidents" \[1\]. He pointed to plaintiff's counsel at oral argument, who said brokers "just have to hire carriers that actually have a reasonable policy," and that a broker "is not going to have a problem if it's asking the hard questions of the carrier" \[1\].


He also agreed with the brokers that state tort law "can be unpredictable," and that litigation and insurance costs "may be significant even when brokers prevail" \[1\]. His answer was that brokers can ask Congress to change the law.


## Where broker liability stands in November 2026


The Supreme Court issued its judgment to the lower court on June 15, 2026 \[3\]. Montgomery's claim against the broker now goes back to the lower courts. We found no public ruling on the remand as of November 18, 2026.


The decision already shows up in other cases. Trade press reported on July 24, 2026 that a Dallas County jury had returned a $604 million verdict over a March 2021 pileup on Interstate 20 in Mississippi that killed three people. The jury found all three defendants negligent and gave the largest share of responsibility to the broker, C.H. Robinson, which said it will appeal \[4\]\[5\]. The broker said the carrier held a Satisfactory FMCSA rating when it was selected. The Transportation Intermediaries Association (TIA) said the jury had access to data about the carrier's prior incidents and safety record "that is not available to the public, including brokers" \[4\].


Two other developments matter:


- An FMCSA standard. TIA asked FMCSA to set a federal carrier selection standard and to publish a list of carriers it considers "high risk" \[6\]. In September 2026, TIA members also pressed Congress for a federal standard \[7\].
- A federal bill. The Motor Carrier Safety Selection Standard Act (H.R. 5337) would set a national standard for vetting a carrier. It was introduced on September 11, 2025, and its last action was a referral to the House Subcommittee on Highways and Transit on September 12, 2025 \[8\]. The 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027.


## What negligent selection means for a broker


A negligent-selection claim usually asks three questions:


1. Did the broker know, or should it have known, that the carrier or driver was unsafe?
2. Did the broker hire them anyway?
3. Did that unsafe condition cause the crash and the injury?


The first question is where your records matter. The plaintiff in Montgomery pointed to a public FMCSA safety rating \[1\]. In the Dallas case, the broker relied on a Satisfactory rating, and the jury still found it negligent \[4\].


A carrier check at onboarding answers part of the question. It does not show who drove the truck on the day of the crash. If the load was re-brokered, or a different driver showed up, the carrier you vetted may not be the carrier that moved the freight.


## Carrier checks to document on every load


FMCSA defines three safety ratings and an unrated status in 49 CFR 385.3 \[9\]:


- Satisfactory: the carrier has adequate safety management controls in place and working.
- Conditional: the carrier lacks adequate controls, which could result in violations of the safety fitness standard.
- Unsatisfactory: the carrier lacks adequate controls, and that has resulted in violations.
- Unrated: FMCSA has not assigned a rating.


A carrier rated Unsatisfactory is generally prohibited from operating a commercial motor vehicle \[10\]. Montgomery was about a Conditional carrier \[1\].


On each load, record what you checked and when:


- Operating authority is active for the type of freight.
- The safety rating, and any out-of-service order.
- Insurance is on file, with limits that fit the load.
- The dispatcher or owner you deal with is who they say they are, and the phone and email belong to the carrier.
- Your written rule for Conditional and unrated carriers, and the reason you accepted one when you did.


Indemni starts from the carrier's DOT number, pulls its authority, safety, and insurance information, and checks the dispatcher's identity, phone, and email \[11\].[See what Indemni checks on a carrier](https://www.indemni.com/platform/carrier-lookup#faq-what-do-we-need-to-look-up-a-carrier)


## Driver and truck checks at pickup


The carrier check happens at booking. A crash happens on the road, with one driver in one truck. A record that stops at the carrier does not show who that driver was.


At or before pickup, check:


- The driver's commercial driver's license (CDL) is authentic and matches the driver assigned to the load.
- The U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) number on the truck door matches the carrier you booked.
- The truck and trailer match the assignment.
- Where the driver is when they verify, compared with the pickup location.


When a check fails, write down what failed, who reviewed it, and what they decided. An override with a reason is a better record than a silent pass.


In Indemni, the driver verifies by phone. Indemni checks the CDL against the assigned driver, reads the USDOT number on the truck door and compares it with the driver's carrier, and your team sees each result, with a time, on the load \[11\].[See how Indemni verifies a driver](https://www.indemni.com/platform/driver-verification#faq-how-does-indemni-verify-a-driver)


## What to do this quarter


1. Write down your carrier selection policy, including how you treat Conditional, unrated, and new carriers.
2. Make sure the policy runs on every load, not only at onboarding.
3. Add a driver and truck check at pickup on loads with a higher risk.
4. Keep each check, its result, the reviewer, and the time on the load, so you can produce it years later.
5. Review your contingent auto liability coverage and your carrier contracts with your broker and counsel.
